title: Seeking Sweet and Sour Feedback
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article focuses on the listening tour a new leader should conduct before making any changes to a team or area they've just taken over. Its central technique is the sweet and sour framing, explicitly asking what's going well and what isn't, which the author argues produces more candid answers than open-ended questions because it signals both positives and negatives are welcome. Starting with the positives is described as a way to build comfort before people share harder criticism. The piece emphasizes that genuine listening, done before any changes are made, is what makes team members feel truly heard.
points: New leaders should conduct a listening tour before making any changes to a team or area
The sweet and sour framing, asking what's best and what's worst, produces more candid feedback
Starting with positives helps people open up before sharing harder criticisms
Changes should wait until after genuine listening has happened, not a minute before
quotes: So, good leaders conduct a listening tour, where they meet with individuals and groups to hear what they have to say.
Resistance is magnified any time a leader makes changes before absorbing the views and opinions of the team members and stakeholders.
Sweet and sour feedback is a powerful metaphor for learning about what is going well and what needs improvement or attention.
Framing the question as seeking sweet and sour feedback is a great setup for asking a two-sided question: What is the best of the place, and what is the worst of the place?
Once they know the current state, leaders are primed to make changes. But not a minute before then.
